summary: Presents functional requirements for deploying IP multicast within Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs, from both customer and provider viewpoints, to guide candidate solutions. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast sends one stream to many viewers. This lists what a provider's private network service must do to support that for its customers.

questions: ip multicast in provider provisioned vpn
what are the requirements for multicast in l3vpn
how does multicast work over a provider vpn
subtitle: What a provider-run Layer 3 VPN must do to carry customers' IP multicast efficiently, securely and at scale.

tldr.problem: Multicast traffic is not natively supported in existing L3 provider-provisioned VPN solutions, and ad hoc workarounds scale badly in operations, state and bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists functional requirements from the customer and service provider viewpoints, backed by a 2005 survey of expected deployments, without specifying any solution.
tldr.outcome: Candidate multicast VPN solutions SHOULD satisfy these requirements. The RFC itself is Informational and defines no protocol.

facts.label: Required CE-PE protocols
facts.value: PIM-SM (including SSM) and IGMPv3 and/or MLDv2

today: RFC 4834 is an Informational RFC from April 2007 and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document for solutions, not a protocol.

sections.title: The Problem and Scope
sections.content:
Layer 3 VPN services meeting the requirements of RFC 4031 are popular because customers need not know the VPN technology and because P (provider) routers need not know VPN details. Meanwhile there is a growing need for IP multicast, built on protocols such as Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) and IGMP.

Multicast is not natively supported by existing L3 PPVPN solutions. Doing it with only standardized solutions means custom designs that are limited in scalability, operational efficiency and bandwidth usage. This document adds multicast-specific requirements to the generic L3VPN ones, stays solution agnostic, and applies equally to IPv4 and IPv6. A solution MUST interoperate seamlessly with current unicast VPN solutions.

The RFC uses the common vocabulary of PE and CE routers, VRF, and a generic MDTunnel (multicast distribution tunnel) for the means of carrying customer multicast across the provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: Private networks for companies work well, but sending one video to many offices is awkward on them today. This note says what a proper fix needs.

sections.title: Use Cases and Scale Targets
sections.content:
Customers want to extend multicast services to remote sites, for example a national TV channel broadcasting from a central point to regional locations. Point-to-point tunnels would make PEs replicate traffic, which scales poorly and wastes bandwidth. There is also a built-in tension between scalability and resource optimization, since optimizing means keeping state for replication trees in the core.

The scenarios come from a summer 2005 survey with 13 responses: live content broadcast, symmetric many-to-many applications such as conferencing, data distribution, and a generic offer where every VPN supports multicast by default.

Scale expectations drawn from it include:

  • from one to several thousands of multicast VPNs
  • several hundreds of multicast VPNs per PE
  • several hundreds of PEs per multicast VPN, possibly thousands
  • hundreds or thousands of streams per VPN, and hundreds per PE
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a TV network sending a show to many offices. The note imagines many such networks at once and asks that the system handle that size.

sections.title: Customer Requirements
sections.content:
Multicast service MUST be provider provisioned and SHALL NOT require customer CE devices to support any extra features beyond non-VPN multicast. CE-PE exchanges SHOULD use existing protocols. Support for PIM-SM (including SSM) and either IGMPv3 (IPv4) and/or MLDv2 (IPv6) is REQUIRED; bidir-PIM is RECOMMENDED and PIM-DM is OPTIONAL.

Other customer-side requirements include:

  • QoS: at least the quality of service available for unicast and for non-VPN multicast, with attention to group join and leave delay, and no lost or duplicated packets where possible.
  • Operations: SLA monitoring, multicast statistics, and customer visibility into their multicast state and throughput.
  • Security: the same level as for unicast, with multicast activation possible per VRF, per CE interface, per group or channel.
  • Extranet: a VRF MUST be able to take part in more than one VPN, with multicast connectivity controllable separately from unicast. Internet multicast is OPTIONAL.
  • Addressing: overlapping multicast group addresses between customers MUST be supported.
  • MTU: encapsulation overhead SHOULD be minimized, and a 1500-byte IP MTU should be allowed when the backbone permits.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers should not have to buy new gear or learn new tricks. Their private broadcasts must stay private, work well, and be easy to watch over.

sections.title: Service Provider Requirements
sections.content:
Deployment SHOULD have little or no impact on existing standardized multicast protocols on P and PE routers. Scalability is a key requirement: solutions MUST scale well with the number of PEs, customer VPNs, sites and multicast channels, ideally keeping the core independent of customer count. Where that cannot be had, state in the core should at least be boundable.

On resource optimization, the RFC says that one size does not fit all. It names two ends of the trade-off space: bandwidth optimization, with core trees that closely follow customer routing but need lots of state, and state optimization, with aggregated MDTunnels that scale better but send traffic to leaves that do not need it. Providers SHOULD get settings to tune this.

The solution MUST let the provider control the number of sources and groups and their bit rate. It MUST support inter-AS multicast VPNs and SHOULD support inter-provider ones. It SHOULD NOT be tied to one tunneling technology: GRE, MPLS (including point-to-multipoint), L2TP, IPsec and IP-in-IP are listed examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The company running the network must be able to grow it big, choose between saving wire space or saving memory, and keep any one customer from hogging things.

sections.title: Operations, Migration and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
The provider SHOULD have multicast traffic statistics, client resource usage, alarms when limits are reached, IP performance metrics such as one-way delay, and information to judge its bandwidth/state trade-off. These SHOULD be exposed through standardized MIB modules with SNMP, or through IPFIX. Alarm generation SHOULD be rate limited, for example with hysteresis.

Unicast and multicast services MUST be able to coexist in the same VPN, activation SHOULD be smooth, and a solution SHOULD state a migration policy. Since adaptive carrying of traffic can be hard to debug, a solution SHOULD provide monitoring that describes how client traffic is carried, and MAY allow dynamic changes to be turned off for a particular VPN or stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need dashboards, quiet alarms, a gentle upgrade path, and clues for finding problems when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it does not by itself raise any particular security issue, but that a set of issues MUST be addressed when designing and deploying multicast-enabled L3 PPVPNs. Customers need security equal to unicast and a way to avoid their traffic reaching PEs outside the VPN. Providers need the same level of protection as for unicast VPNs, including traffic segregation and protection against DoS attacks, bounded rates of change in how traffic is carried, and traffic of a channel with no members in a VPN MUST NOT be propagated in it. For inter-AS use, integrity and authenticity of multicast exchanges is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast must be as safe as normal private traffic. Nothing should leak to networks that did not ask for it, and attackers should not easily overload the system.
